note: A title matching a phrase does not make the judgment about this project. Open it, check the parties, the parcel and the dates, and drop it if the harm it records is not the card's harm. An empty result is not an absence either: the phrase may be wrong. Try the parties' names from the card.

card.title: 239 People Unpaid When the Kampala Roads Credit Closed

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit C4367 of US$33.6 million for the Kampala Institutional and Infrastructure Development Project (P078382), approved by the Board on 6 November 2007. Original closing was 31 December 2010; after two extensions totalling three years the project closed on 31 December 2013. Project costs were US$37.10 million at appraisal. A restructuring approved on 3 December 2010 extended the closing date by 24 months and created an additional category of eligible expenditure for involuntary resettlement, because the government could no longer fully finance the project's resettlement cost; a second restructuring on 27 December 2012 extended closing again from 31 December 2012 to 31 December 2013. Environmental category B. The implementing agency was Kampala City Council, which became the Kampala Capital City Authority during the project. The Independent Evaluation Group's review rated outcome Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Moderate and quotes the completion report by paragraph (IEG ICR Review ICRR14588, date posted 25 February 2015).

companies.name: Kampala City Council, later the Kampala Capital City Authority
companies.role: The city government of Kampala and the project's implementing agency; in 2011 the elected City Council was replaced by the Capital City Authority, a central-government body under a minister, with an Executive Director appointed by the president. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says a lack of capacity in the Council and Authority, compounded by insufficient government funding for the resettlement compensation, led to the compensation problems, and that the body had no specialist to handle safeguard issues (IEG ICR Review, 25 February 2015).
companies.desc: The city government of Kampala, Uganda. The Kampala Capital City Act, assented to on 28 December 2010, published in Uganda Gazette 2 on 14 January 2011 and commenced on 1 March 2011 by the Kampala Capital City (Commencement) Instrument 2011, provides in section 5(1) for an Authority known as the Kampala Capital City Authority, a body corporate which section 5(3) makes the governing body of the Capital City, administering it on behalf of the central government, and provides in section 4(2) that any entity which immediately before the commencement existed as a local government in the delineated area ceases to be a local government. Its chief executive is an executive director appointed by the President on the advice of the Public Service Commission (section 17), and under section 79 the minister responsible for the capital city may vary or rescind, with Cabinet's approval, any decision of the Authority that contravenes any law or Government policy, and has general powers to give directives on policy and general development which the Authority must comply with.

card.community: The credit paid for rebuilding city roads, traffic junctions and drainage channels in Kampala together with reform of the city government. The resettlement action plan of October 2006 set out two design scenarios and recorded that under the second, which the City Council accepted for implementation, 415 entities, meaning individuals, households and businesses, were affected and 141 of them would relocate, some on the same plot and some to a wholly new site, with an extra 15 per cent on the value of the property allowed for the cost of moving. The plan's eligible categories ran from registered title holders down to licensees, those with the landowner's permission to put up a kiosk or grow seasonal crops but no legal claim, and squatters with neither legal nor customary claim. Its cut-off date was 15 April 2006. The plan set out a three-stage grievance procedure starting at the division office. Its table of the adopted scenario puts 91 of the 141 relocations on one work, the Lubigi primary channel, which runs through Kawaala; the rest are spread over five roads, four other drains and two traffic junctions. Its census counted 1,118 people in the corridor, 623 of them, 55 per cent, renting the premises for business, residence or both and 495, 45 per cent, claiming to own the property, and it put vulnerable households, those headed by women over 60, by very young women and by the unemployed, at 10 per cent. The Independent Evaluation Group's review gives the outcome: by the project's closing date of 31 December 2013, 494 project-affected persons had been compensated and 239 persons had yet to receive compensation. It attributes most of the outstanding payments, citing the completion report's paragraph 48, to unsubstantiated claims, and says that by the time the completion report was concluded all eligible claims had been paid off. On the environmental side it records deficiencies in safeguard implementation, especially at the landfill: poor handling of the landfill acquisition with no proper due diligence before the six-acre extension land was bought, incomplete fencing around the site, reliance on a temporary operating licence for longer than expected, and a leachate monitoring and treatment system not commensurate with the national waste water treatment and discharge standard, posing health and safety risks to the public. It says all of those were resolved within a month of the project closing.
card.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the Independent Evaluation Group's review.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,118 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. That figure is in the project's own resettlement action plan of October 2006, to the person: the plan's census counted 1,118 people in the corridor, 623 renting and 495 claiming ownership. The project's own resettlement action plan of October 2006 counted 415 affected entities, meaning individuals, households and businesses, of whom 141 were to relocate under the design the City Council adopted. The Independent Evaluation Group's review counts 494 people compensated and 239 not compensated by the closing date, 733 in all. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
card.outcome: The credit closed on 31 December 2013 with 239 people still unpaid. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says that by the time the completion report was concluded all eligible claims had been paid, attributing most of the outstanding payments to unsubstantiated claims, and rated the project's outcome Satisfactory. The Bank went on to lend for a Second Kampala Institutional and Infrastructure Development Project, approved 20 March 2014, under which an Inspection Panel case was later registered over the Lubigi drainage channel at Kawaala, the work that carried 91 of the 141 relocations planned under this first credit.
card.confidence_note: The project's own completion report is not disclosed. Searches of the Bank's document archive under this project number, by title and by project name returned no completion report, so the figures of 494 compensated and 239 unpaid rest entirely on the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report, which cites it by paragraph. The lender is therefore reporting on its own project at one remove, and the underlying document cannot be checked. Searches for Ugandan press or non-governmental reports on compensation under this first Kampala project found only material about its successor, the second project approved in 2014. No document found names any of the 239 people, says how long they waited, says which roads they were on, or says how many of them were among the 141 who were to relocate. The review says that by the time the completion report was concluded all eligible claims had been paid off and rated the project's outcome Satisfactory. The 415 affected entities and 141 relocations are planning figures from the October 2006 plan, not outcomes.

card.whole: The completion report records that the project expanded and lined 3.6 kilometres of the Lubigi primary drainage channel, its target, and upgraded gravel roads to bitumen standard on 11.81 kilometres of the about 14.42 kilometres planned at approval, of which 8.73 kilometres was fully complete and open at closing against a target revised to 12.89 kilometres, the rest being finished by the city council itself by the end of May 2014. It developed six acres of land next to the existing landfill, trained 76 staff in contract management and revenue collection, bought 25 vehicles along with information technology and records management equipment, extended the council's network to division offices, carried out its financial recovery plan, completed a strategic planning process and five public consultations, and updated the Kampala Physical Development Plan. The city council's stock of overdue liabilities fell from UGX 8 billion to zero against an original target of UGX 3 billion and a revised UGX 0.5 billion, though the report adds that UGX 2.6 billion was still recorded as a liability with no supporting documents for the claims and was to be written off after verification. Own-source revenue rose from UGX 22 billion in 2005/06 to UGX 55.71 billion in 2012/13, against an original target of UGX 30 billion and a revised UGX 33.5 billion, and the report puts its average annual growth at 12.2 per cent during the project against 6.4 per cent in the seven years before it. The share of own-source revenue spent on service delivery reached 32.7 per cent against 10 per cent at the start, an original target of 30 per cent and a revised 34. Building permit approval fell from a year in 2006 to two months, the share of property owners issued rate demand notes rose from 30 per cent in 2006 to 100 per cent in 2013, traffic on the upgraded roads grew 31 per cent against a revised target of 20 per cent on an indicator added at restructuring, and the number of people affected by floods along the Lubigi channel fell from 8,800 to none. Public satisfaction, the fourth outcome indicator, was not met on any of its three measures: roads 29 per cent against a target of 50, drainage 22 per cent against 31 and solid waste 46 per cent against 60, and the report notes that the figures come from citizens report card surveys covering services across Kampala rather than the project's own works. Works were dropped at the first restructuring, in December 2010: the secondary drainage channels, 4 kilometres of them, and four tertiary drainage black spots, both recorded at zero; the area traffic management works; the landfill gas collection and flaring system; the maintenance of about 26 kilometres of tarmac roads, recorded as zero against 374.07 kilometres of bitumen roads to be improved, after a national road fund took over road maintenance; and the infrastructure for the Kibuli and Kawempe markets. A human resources management system was dropped when a national payroll system was rolled out, and a complaints management system, customer care desks, a client charter and a perceptions survey were not implemented. The report says the money was moved to cover resettlement costs under the resettlement action plan, extended consultancies and higher operating costs, the government's own contribution having fallen short. The report puts the economic rate of return on the road works at 29.8 per cent at completion against 32 per cent at appraisal: three of the five roads returned more than the 12 per cent discount rate, while Kimera returned 7.9 per cent with a net present value of minus US$0.378 million and Soweto 9.6 per cent with minus US$0.256 million, which the report attributes to actual construction costs per kilometre more than twice the estimate. The return on the Lubigi channel was 17.5 per cent at completion, against 14.0 per cent at appraisal in the report's table and 16.8 per cent in the Evaluation Group's review. The report rates efficiency Satisfactory and the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the review rates efficiency Substantial and the outcome Satisfactory. On the institutional side the report sets US$1.62 million of spending against a UGX 33.71 billion rise in own-source revenue and calls the efficiency potentially very high, while the review says the efficiency of that spending cannot be assessed, for want of information on what the council itself spent to raise its revenue and of any benchmark for an efficient revenue collection system. The project cost US$35.64 million against US$37.10 million at appraisal, with US$33.58 million of the US$33.6 million credit disbursed and US$2.06 million of the US$3.5 million expected from the government provided, and the closing date was extended twice, by three years in total. All these figures are the lender's own; no check from outside the World Bank Group was found.
card.conditions: The project was environmental category B, which triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment and natural habitats, and the policy on involuntary resettlement was also triggered. An environmental analysis with an environmental management plan was prepared at preparation stage, and a detailed resettlement action plan dated October 2006. The plan valued land and permanent structures at market value, which it says is higher than replacement cost in the city, and used the Council's 2003 rates for temporary and semi-permanent structures and crops. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the Council and Authority had limited capacity and lacked a specialist to handle safeguard issues. Because the government could no longer fully finance the resettlement cost, the restructuring approved on 3 December 2010 created a new category of eligible expenditure under the credit for involuntary resettlement (IEG ICR Review, 25 February 2015; Resettlement Action Plan, October 2006).

card.title: Deaths and Unapproved Displacement on the Mafinga-Igawa Road
card.place: Mafinga-Igawa road, Iringa and Mbeya regions, Tanzania

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Southern Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project, first phase (P120370), Credit IDA-52480 of SDR 138.7 million (US$210 million equivalent) to Tanzania and Grant IDA-H8440 of SDR 2.0 million (US$3 million) to the Dar es Salaam Corridor Committee, approved 21 May 2013, effective 26 November 2013, closed 31 December 2020 after two extensions; US$175.4 million disbursed. The rehabilitation of the 137.9 km Mafinga-Igawa section of the Dar es Salaam corridor took 78 per cent of the project's money; for the remaining stretch to the Zambian border at Tunduma the project paid only for feasibility studies, detailed designs and safeguard instruments. The project also financed a one-stop border post at Songwe/Kasumulu on the Malawi border, an inspection station at Vigwaza and works at eight accident black spots. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory (28 January 2022); the Evaluation Group rates Bank performance and the quality of supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory, records that the project closed with a moderately unsatisfactory rating for safeguards, and says it is not clear how the Bank "addressed the issue of fatalities related to contractors and ensured that such accidents did not repeat".

companies.name: Tanzania National Roads Agency (TANROADS)
companies.role: Implementing agency for the road works, the border post and the black spot works; began work at one black spot, including displacing people, without preparing the safeguard documents
companies.desc: An executive agency under Tanzania's works ministry that manages and maintains the national trunk and regional road network through regional offices.

card.community: Twenty-four people died along the Mafinga-Igawa road while it was being rehabilitated. The completion report counts 104 accidents on the project road during construction, 13 of them fatal, and says that of the 24 deaths "two were attributed to the contractors' employees or involved contractors' employees and/or equipment, with the rest due to road crashes". The report puts the rate at 0.06 deaths per kilometre per year, half the Tanzanian average of 0.11 for trunk roads at the time, which it links to the slower speeds through the works, and then calls that rate "undoubtedly shocking". A road safety audit was carried out and its findings went into the road design. The borrower's comments, printed in the same report, dispute the Bank's account: they give the number as 23, say that calling it a large number "is not evidenced", point out that the report itself records the rate as below the national average, and say there is no evidence for the implied conclusion that the contractors' handling of traffic was insufficient for the traffic on the corridor. On land, the report says resettlement plans were prepared and carried out satisfactorily for most of the works, but that problems remained at closing in two places. At the one-stop border post, "compensation and demolition of property required by the implementation occurred prior to clearance of the RAP". At one of the black spot sites, "works began, including displacement without preparation of safeguards instruments by TANROADS and approval by the WB". The Bank says it kept monitoring after the project closed to ensure its resettlement policy was met and the affected people properly compensated, and that it will do so until all the resettlement issues are addressed. Other safeguard failures the report and the review record are a contractor dumping debris in wetlands and blocking water flow, and diversion roads built for the works left unattended, with erosion then affecting more than 20 km along the corridor.
card.killed_note: The completion report counts 24 deaths along the Mafinga-Igawa road during construction, from 104 accidents of which 13 were fatal. Two are counted here because the report ties them to the contractors: they were "attributed to the contractors' employees or involved contractors' employees and/or equipment". The other 22 the report puts down to road crashes and they are not counted. The borrower's comments in the same report give the total as 23.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 17 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people. No World Bank document for this project counts the people displaced at the border post or at the black spot.
card.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2020 with the border post and the inspection station at Vigwaza still unfinished, to be completed with government money. The time for trucks to cross from Songwe into Malawi rose from 24 hours at appraisal to 72 hours at closing, which the report puts down to the construction still under way and to Covid-19 controls. The resettlement and compensation problems at the border post and at the black spot were unresolved when the project closed, and the project's safeguards rating at closing was Moderately Unsatisfactory.
card.confidence_note: The deaths, the demolition before the resettlement plan was cleared and the displacement without safeguard documents are all recorded in the World Bank's own completion report and in its Evaluation Group's review of that report. The borrower disputes the Bank's account of the deaths in the same report, giving 23 rather than 24 and rejecting the implied conclusion about the contractors. No document names the people displaced or counts them. No independent report was found.

sources.title: Southern Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR00005186)
ICR Review: SA Trade and Transport Facilitation Project (ICRR0022904)
Financing Agreement, Credit 5248-TZ, Southern Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project
Project Agreement, Credit 5248-TZ, Southern Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project

card.whole: The project rebuilt the 137.9 km Mafinga-Igawa section of the Dar es Salaam corridor, which took 78 per cent of its money, and US$175.4 million was spent. The time for a container to cross Tanzania on the corridor fell from 7 days to 2, as measured by the Tanzania Revenue Authority, though the report says in the same paragraph that much of that gain is now lost to longer waits at the border during the border post works. Freight on the corridor rose from 35,000 containers a year at appraisal to 81,478 at closing, and daily traffic at the Makambako counting station from 1,716 vehicles in 2011 to 4,444 in 2020, with trucks up from 821 to 1,339. Of 20 roadside health clinics planned, 5 were finished by closing and treated 7,425 patients against a target of 3,000; the figures come from the lender and the borrower's own agencies, with no independent check found.
card.conditions: The financing agreement of 30 July 2013 required Tanzania to carry out the project in accordance with the safeguards documents, which the agreement defines as including the abbreviated resettlement plan for the Mafinga-Igawa road section published on 11 October 2012 and the resettlement policy framework of the same date (World Bank, Financing Agreement for Credit 5248-TZ, Schedule 2, Section I.D). Where an activity in the annual work plan needed a resettlement plan, the agreement barred it from being implemented until the plan had been prepared, disclosed and approved by the Association, until all measures the plan required before the work started had been taken, until a report on compliance satisfactory to the Association had been given to it, and until "the Association has confirmed that said activities may be commenced". The government could not abrogate, amend, repeal, suspend, waive or fail to enforce the safeguards documents without the Association's written agreement.

card.title: Unsettled Resettlement Cases at Bukoba Airport

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-47240 and IDA-49910 for the Transport Sector Support Project (P055120), SDR 214.3 million in all, US$329 million equivalent: US$270 million under IDA-47240, of which US$266.20 million was disbursed, and US$59 million under IDA-49910, of which US$54.40 million was disbursed, the second being the additional financing approved 30 June 2011 and carried under its own number P126206. Approved 27 May 2010, effective 1 December 2010, mid-term review 5 May 2014, closing extended from 30 June 2015 to 20 June 2017. The borrower was to contribute US$11.7 million and contributed US$4.51 million, for a total project cost of US$325.12 million against US$340.7 million planned. The project financed roads under Component A and airports, including Bukoba, Kigoma, Tabora and Zanzibar, under Component B. Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) and Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11) were triggered. The completion report rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and quality of monitoring and evaluation Modest; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021116, dated 25 May 2018, gave the same three ratings with no disagreement recorded and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial. The completion report's data sheet names only the Tanzania National Roads Agency as implementing agency; the report adds that TANROADS was the principal implementing agency and handled overall coordination, while the Tanzania Airports Authority implemented the regional airports under Component B and the Government of Zanzibar the Zanzibar airport.

companies.name: Tanzania Airports Authority
companies.role: The government executive agency that operates Tanzania's government-owned airports and was responsible for the airport component. Its establishment order, G.N. No. 404 of 1999, makes it an executive agency in relation to the Department of Aerodromes and gives its role as to "operate, manage, maintain and develop Government-owned airports"; the airports are government-owned and the agency operates them. Resettlement plans were prepared for all the airports in the project, and at project closure the entitlement agreed in the one Bukoba case settled through the grievance mechanism was still awaiting payment from this authority, which agreed to keep sending progress reports to the Bank until the remaining cases were resolved.
companies.desc: A Tanzanian government executive agency established on 29 November 1999 by the Executive Agencies (Tanzania Airports Authority) (Establishment) Order, G.N. No. 404 of 1999, as an executive agency "in relation to the Department of Aerodromes". Its framework document gives its role as to "operate, manage, maintain and develop Government-owned airports in a professional and cost-effective manner", and names the Minister for Communications and Transport as the responsible minister.

companies.name: Tanzania National Roads Agency
companies.role: The executive agency responsible for Tanzania's trunk and regional roads, which implemented the road component and held fiduciary responsibility for the project, and which hired three additional procurement staff for it.
companies.desc: A Tanzanian government executive agency whose roles the national audit office cites from Rule 3(3) of the Executive Agencies (The Tanzania National Roads Agency) (Amendment) Order No. 350 of 2009, and whose performance on road maintenance the Ministry of Works and Transport oversees. The Roads Act, 2007 requires it, as a roads authority, to prepare and implement short and long-term road maintenance programmes. The audit, citing the Roads Fund Board's annual report of June 2019, records it as maintaining a national network of 36,258 km — 12,176 km of trunk roads and 24,082 km of regional roads, of which 1,756 km were paved.

card.community: The project paved and improved runways, taxiways, aprons and terminals at Bukoba, Kigoma, Tabora and Zanzibar airports and rehabilitated road lengths. The completion report rates the project's social safeguard management satisfactory. It states that resettlement plans were prepared for all the airports, that no resettlement was required at Tabora or Kigoma, that resettlement at Zanzibar airport was completed, and that at Bukoba five resettlement cases remained pending at project closure. Four of those five were awaiting court deliberations. The fifth had been resolved through the project's grievance redress mechanism, with the entitlement agreed and payment still pending from the Tanzania Airports Authority. The authority agreed to keep submitting progress reports to the Bank until the remaining cases were resolved. During implementation it was found that Tumaini Primary School, a public primary school serving the area around Bukoba airport and hosting a unit for more than 50 disabled children, stood within the flight path of the extended runway. Flight restrictions were imposed so that operations were allowed only in the direction away from the school, and it was decided that the school had to be relocated. Empty land was contributed by the local government, new school buildings were put up, and both former and new students began attending in the new location; the original school was demolished and its land demarcated. The completion report says there were some students whose commute was made more challenging but that the move was largely successful, and that the airports authority and the Bukoba airport management committed to continue supporting the school. On the road component, the lengths were built inside existing alignments and no resettlement was found to be required; the 7 km stretch of the Arusha to Minjingo road inside Arusha town was left out of the civil works at preparation because resettlement would have been needed there, although the detailed designs for it were finished. During implementation several families living near a quarry used by the Arusha to Minjingo contractor asked to be relocated; the report says their request was met and they were relocated. At Zanzibar airport the extension of the taxiway required a cemetery to be relocated, which the report says was done satisfactorily. No archaeologist was engaged as the project had expected, although the report says very little undisturbed land was used and no chance finds were identified.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,595 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated. The only figures in the Bank's documents are five resettlement cases still pending at Bukoba at project closure, four of them in court, and several unnumbered families near a quarry on the Arusha to Minjingo road who asked to be relocated and were.
card.outcome: The credits closed on 20 June 2017, two years after the original closing date. Five resettlement cases at Bukoba were still unresolved at closure, four of them before the courts and one with payment outstanding. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that the project team subsequently told it that the high court cases on carrying out the resettlement plan had been ruled on and that payment of compensation to the affected people was being processed; that statement is attributed to the project team and not to a document. The completion report of 16 January 2018 rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.
card.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the Bank's own completion report on its own project and from the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. No independent source on the Bukoba resettlement cases or the school was found. The documents give no count of people, name nobody, do not say how much the outstanding entitlement was or what the four court cases were about, and do not say how many students' journeys to school became longer. The later statement that the court cases had been decided and payment was being processed is attributed to the project team rather than to a document. The completion report also says the school move was largely successful, that the families near the quarry asked to move and were satisfied, and that the Zanzibar resettlement was completed. The completion report's cover page is dated January 16, 2017, five months before the closing date of 20 June 2017 that its own data sheet gives; the Independent Evaluation Group's review states that the date on the front page should be 2018 and not 2017, and the report's exchange rate is given as effective 27 December 2017.

card.whole: The project rehabilitated or maintained 909 kilometres of road, 268 kilometres under the roads component against a target of 270 and 641 kilometres with 212 culverts and two bridges under emergency maintenance in 19 of Tanzania's 31 regions, about 14 per cent of the national paved network, and rebuilt four airports. Vehicle operating costs fell from US$0.34 to US$0.22 a kilometre on the Korogwe-Same road against a target of US$0.23 and from US$0.45 to US$0.27 on Arusha-Minjingu against US$0.25; the share of classified roads in good or fair condition is given as 86 per cent against a target of 70, with the completion report stating that inconsistency in how the indicator was measured makes the achievement difficult to assess. At Bukoba the runway was extended and paved, a new terminal built after the old one was condemned following an earthquake, and the airport rated able to take ATR-42 aircraft; its traffic reached 33,138 passengers in 2016 against a target of 34,000 and a baseline of 26,628, and the average number of passengers per aircraft rose from 8.6 in 2009 to 18.6 in 2017. Of the other three airports Zanzibar carried 946,905 passengers against a target of 660,000, Kigoma 29,781 against 40,000 and Tabora 16,505 against 30,000, below its baseline of 22,912, which the report attributes to restrictions on operations during the extended works. Ex-post economic rates of return were 18.3 per cent at Bukoba against 15 per cent at appraisal, 8.5 per cent at Kigoma against 23 per cent and minus 9.6 per cent at Tabora, and 17.1 per cent on the Korogwe-Same road against 19 and 19.9 per cent at appraisal and 16.3 per cent on Arusha-Minjingu against 15.2; the report rated efficiency Modest. All these figures are the lender's own; no independent check was found.
card.conditions: The project triggered Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12) and Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11). Resettlement action plans were prepared for every airport in the project. The 7 km of the Arusha to Minjingo road inside Arusha town was deliberately excluded from the civil works at preparation because resettlement would have been required there, while the detailed designs for a later rehabilitation were completed. The project was expected to engage an archaeologist to assess chance finds under the cultural property policy and did not do so. Construction companies were required to put in place HIV prevention education and sensitisation plans, including voluntary testing, in collaboration with district health officers (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 16 January 2018; ICR Review ICRR0021116, 25 May 2018).

card.title: Lower Nzoia irrigation: 568 people unpaid at closing and two drownings
card.place: Lower Nzoia irrigation scheme and flood dykes, Busia and Siaya counties, Kenya

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-52680 (US$155 million), IDA-56740 (US$58 million) and IDA-74230 (US$30 million) and trust fund TF-A0761 (US$3.5 million) for the Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635). Approved 18 June 2013, effective 24 October 2013, closed 31 May 2025. Bank financing of US$243 million was revised down to US$141.24 million with US$147.32 million disbursed. Credits were partly cancelled at restructurings on 4 September 2017 and 25 June 2019 and the closing date was extended three times (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 December 2025).

lenders.name: KfW (Germany)
lenders.role: US$20.01 million in the original financing plan, revised to nil, with US$14,985 recorded as disbursed (World Bank completion report).

card.community: The Bank's completion report says that at project closure, 'of the 4,704 PAPs, 88 percent were compensated, while the remaining were 568 PAPs (12 percent) with a value of around US$883,000', and attributes the shortfall to absentee claimants, succession grants, pending affidavits and missing title documents. It says the borrower remains liable and that the National Land Commission must secure and ringfence the money until the unpayable claimants become eligible. It also records 156 grievances about compensation, safeguards, construction and access, of which 142 were resolved; of the 14 left, 11 were about pending compensation. The report says the processes for preparing and clearing the four resettlement plans and for paying compensation took a considerable time and were flagged as contributing to delays across the project. The Star reported on 8 November 2022 that residents of Ugunja, Alego Usonga and Ugenya sub-counties in Siaya and Budalang'i in Busia accepted the project but objected to the 7-metre-wide tertiary canals, which would leave smallholders with little or no land, feared the government would not pay for the land taken for them, and wanted to know where they would be relocated; it says compensation for the main and secondary canals had largely been settled from Ugunja to Block 7 in Usonga ward while the tertiary canals remained unresolved, and that the National Land Commission's compensation gazette notice was dated 21 June 2021.
card.killed_note: Two deaths by drowning during the project's construction period, recorded in the World Bank's completion report, which says all construction work was immediately suspended, an investigation into the causes was carried out and corrective actions were taken. Neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group's review says who drowned or where.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 9,079 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives 4,704 project-affected persons, of whom 88 per cent were compensated and 568 were not, with no breakdown between people who lost land and people who lost homes and no count of anyone relocated. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the same figures. No figure is entered here because no document found counts anyone relocated. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
card.outcome: The Bank's two documents on this project say different things about its resettlement performance, and both are given here. The completion report says the project complied with the resettlement policy OP 4.12 and that the social safeguards rating 'mostly remained Moderately Satisfactory' including at closing. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of the same report says 'the rating for Involuntary Resettlement was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory (MU) by 2018 and remained MU until 2022 when it was upgraded to Moderately Satisfactory', with the other social safeguard policies staying moderately satisfactory. At closing 568 claimants worth about US$883,000 were still unpaid, and the Bank said it would monitor the post-closure safeguard action plan twice a year, including through the follow-on project. Of the irrigation works, supporting structures for a second phase were built, and the completion report records that land compensation and related social and environmental problems delayed handing sites to the contractor.
card.confidence_note: The unpaid compensation and the two drownings are stated only in the World Bank's own completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it, which are the lender reporting on its own project; no independent record of the unpaid claimants or the deaths was found. The Star's report is about a different part of the scheme, the land the 7-metre tertiary canals would take and where the people losing it would go, and does not cover the 568 unpaid claimants or the drownings, so it does not corroborate them. No document found counts anyone relocated under this project, so the harm recorded here is unpaid and late compensation and the two deaths, not a completed resettlement.

sources.title: Kenya - Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
Kenya - KE Enhancing Water Security & Climate Resilience: ICR Review (ICRR0024889)
Land tussles threaten Sh5.3bn Nzoia irrigation project

card.whole: By the Bank's own count the scheme gave 2,457 hectares new or improved irrigation and drainage, which the Independent Evaluation Group puts at 79 per cent of the revised target of 3,095 hectares, against an original target of 4,043 hectares, and reached 8,142 farmers against a revised target of 11,133. The project built 34 km of flood dykes, a target cut from 44 km, and counts 66,700 people with increased flood protection; produce marketed from the scheme was worth US$7.3 million against a target of 2,683 million Kenyan shillings, about US$30 million. The economic rate of return was 14.6 per cent at appraisal, counting gains in crop yields and market value over 20 years at a 12 per cent discount rate, and 13.81 per cent at closing, worked out over 30 years at a 6 per cent discount rate, so the two rates rest on different assumptions; the review also records re-estimates of 13.8 per cent at the 2015 additional financing, 8.9 per cent when US$70 million was cancelled in 2019 and 24.61 per cent at the 2023 additional financing. The review records that 85 to 90 per cent of the project's new or upgraded monitoring stations stopped working about one and a half to two years after installation for want of maintenance money, so the flood forecasting and early warning system they fed could no longer function, and that the government undertook to finish the remaining 22 per cent of the irrigation scheme from its own budget. Both the Bank and the Evaluation Group rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and efficiency Modest. The figures are the lender's own; no independent check of them was found.
card.conditions: The project triggered the Bank's involuntary resettlement and environmental assessment policies, along with pest management and physical cultural resources. Four resettlement action plans were prepared by the borrower and cleared by the Bank, for the Lower Nzoia irrigation scheme, the flood infrastructure and the Mombasa water distribution network. The project was restructured to allow land compensation to be paid from IDA funds through a special-purpose account separate from the government's pooled land compensation account, which meant a National Land Commission bank account had to be opened for the purpose.

card.title: Kenya 1991 University Fees Under the World Bank Education Adjustment Credit
card.place: Public universities across Kenya; point at Nairobi

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Education Sector Adjustment Credit (Cr. 2295-KE) of SDR 75.9 million (US$100 million), approved on 13 September 1991 and closed on 10 March 1995; with IDA reflows it grew to US$203.4 million.

card.community: Students at public universities paid a direct charge of KSh 6,000 for the first time from 1991, when the report's currency table gives KSh 28 to the US dollar. By 1995 the government announced charges of up to KSh 50,000 a year for students judged able to pay, with means-tested loans of up to KSh 42,000 for others (World Bank ICR). The report says public universities fell into arrears from 1992/93.
card.suppression: The Social Conflict Analysis Database (University of Texas) records a nationwide student protest against the raising of university fees on 30 June–1 July 1991 and codes it as met with lethal force, with one death. No news report of this protest was found to confirm it.
card.killed_note: Not counted: the Social Conflict Analysis Database codes one death in the 30 June–1 July 1991 fee protests, but no news report or other source confirming the death, its place or circumstances was found.
card.outcome: The completion report rated progress on student loan reform as 'negligible' during the credit and said that because of high inflation the KSh 6,000 charge fell to about 5% of unit costs by 1995, before the new cost-sharing policy was announced to secure the third tranche (World Bank ICR).
card.confidence_note: The World Bank's own report documents the fee as a condition for presenting the credit to its Board in September 1991, and the fee was charged from the 1991/92 academic year. The protest and the single death come only from the SCAD dataset's coding, so the death is not counted.

sources.title: Development Credit Agreement (Education Sector Adjustment Credit), Credit No. 2295-KE
Student Loans in Kenya: Past Experiences, Current Hurdles, and Opportunities for the Future (Otieno, JHEA/RESA 2(2))

card.whole: The credit agreement made release of each tranche conditional on keeping new public university intake to no more than 10,300 in 1992/93 and 10,600 in 1993/94, and capping student loans at KSh 21,500 (IDA credit agreement, 1991). A later study found that in 1994 the government still bore up to 92% of university costs and households as little as 8%; loan recovery was 3.3% when the Higher Education Loans Board was set up in 1995 and over 18% by 2000–01; public university enrolment grew more than 400% between 1987 and 2000 while government funding rose about 30% (Otieno, 2004). The same study found the richest fifth of households supplied 45% of university students and the poorest fifth 8% (1994 data).
card.conditions: The World Bank's completion report states that before the credit there were 'no direct charges to students at public universities', and that 'a direct charge of KSh. 6000 was introduced for the first time under the credit (this was a condition for Board presentation)', together with a bursary scheme for poor students. The credit also aimed to reform the student loan scheme, which had worked mainly as a grant. Release of the third tranche was tied to a commitment to new financing measures from 1995, under which 'non-needy' students could pay up to 42% of direct costs, about KSh 50,000 a year, and all students a minimum KSh 8,000 towards tuition (World Bank ICR, 1995).
